How did the fur trade change relations between Europeans and Indians and among Indian peoples?
column2: European metal tools and weapons made Indians eager allies of traders like Champlain, while Dutch guns let the Iroquois destroy the Hurons and scatter dozens of peoples in the Beaver Wars, creating a refugee crisis.

column1: Who actually trapped and supplied the furs in New France's fur trade?
column2: New France's Indian allies, chiefly the Hurons, Montagnais and Algonquins, supplied tens of thousands of beaver pelts in exchange for European goods, while the few French traded and lived among them.

column1: What did France aim for in North America?
column2: France sought a permanent presence (Port Royal, then Quebec), profits from the fur trade, and the conversion of Indians to Catholicism, while keeping Canada Catholic and closed to French Protestants.

column1: What made the Jesuits successful among New France's Indians, and what did it do to the Hurons?
column2: Champlain made trading partners let the Jesuits live among them from the 1630s and smallpox drove desperate Hurons to convert, but the conversions divided the Huron confederacy and left it vulnerable to the Iroquois.

column1: What caused the Beaver Wars?
column2: The beaver in Iroquois lands collapsed, Mohawk control of the Dutch trade at Fort Orange gave the Iroquois guns, and epidemics drove them to seize Huron furs, hunting grounds and captives to replace their dead.

column1: How did the Iroquois League gain power in the 1600s?
column2: The five-nation Iroquois confederacy controlled the fur supply to the Dutch at Fort Orange, armed itself with Dutch muskets, destroyed the Hurons and absorbed captives and refugees to replace its dead.

column1: Why did the Indians of the Great Lakes and Mississippi valley welcome French traders?
column2: These peoples wanted French trade goods and help against the Iroquois they feared and hated, and the French also mediated disputes among them.

column1: Along which river did France build the core of New France?
column2: France built its core along the St. Lawrence River, where Cartier first sailed, Champlain founded Quebec, and the towns of Quebec, Montreal and Trois-Rivières stood by 1700.

column1: Why did the French expand into the Mississippi valley?
column2: The Beaver Wars wrecked Champlain's trading system and scattered refugees west, so the French sought new partners and saw the Mississippi valley as the strategic key to North America, hoping its Indian allies would hem in Spain and England.

column1: What contrast does the chapter draw between French and English colonizers?
column2: The French were relatively few and came mainly for trade and converts, while English colonists, spurred in New England by the Protestant Reformation, came in growing numbers and wanted land.

column1: How did predestination shape the Puritans' drive to reform society?
column2: Because the Puritans believed an all-powerful God directed history, they strove to play their part in God's plan by reforming church and society along Calvin's lines.

column1: How did the Separatists differ from other Congregationalists?
column2: The Separatists wanted to leave the Church of England because they thought it too corrupt to reform, while most Congregationalists wanted to stay and reform it.

column1: Who settled the earliest New England colonies?
column2: Separatist Pilgrims, humble craftworkers and farmers, settled Plymouth, and then larger numbers of Puritan Congregationalists and Presbyterians, including merchants, gentlemen and lawyers, settled Massachusetts Bay.

column1: Why did Plymouth survive its first year?
column2: An epidemic had emptied the coast, so the Wampanoag chief Massasoit, eager for trade and allies, helped the starving Pilgrims through the go-between Squanto.

column1: Why did the Massachusetts Bay Puritans come, and how did John Winthrop envision their colony?
column2: Persecuted under King Charles I, the Puritans regrouped across the Atlantic to build an example society, which John Winthrop called a godly "city on a hill" whose settlers "must be knit together, in this work, as one man."

column1: How did New England migrants differ from Chesapeake migrants?
column2: New Englanders came in family groups of skilled, literate farmers, artisans and merchants with a balanced sex ratio, while Chesapeake migrants were mostly young single indentured servants.

column1: How did religion shape New England's government and community life?
column2: Tax-supported churches were the center of community life and policed morality, church membership at first decided who could vote, and settlers sought an ordered society modeled on Scripture, though ministers held no civil office.

column1: What were the sources of stability in early New England?
column2: Family migration, long lives, rough equality of land, strong fathers, shared Puritan churches and broad self-government in town meetings and elected assemblies kept early New England stable.

column1: What were the sources of conflict in early New England?
column2: Fervent disagreement over how to apply the Bible bred dissenters and breakaway colonies, fear of independent women fed witchcraft accusations, and hunger for land led to wars with the Indians.

column1: Why were Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson threats to the Puritan leaders?
column2: Williams attacked ties to the Church of England, church-state union and the king's land charter, while Hutchinson, a woman teaching her own doctrine, challenged the ministers' authority and was branded a heretic.

column1: What happened in the Salem witch hysteria?
column2: In 1692 a group of Salem Village girls' fortune-telling went sour, their fits were blamed on witchcraft, hundreds were accused and twenty innocent people executed until ministers protested.

column1: What weaknesses did New England's Indians face against the colonists?
column2: Epidemics had killed up to 90 percent of coastal peoples, power was local to each village sachem, and rival nations' feuds let the English play them against one another.

column1: What brought about the Pequot War, and how did it end?
column2: Seeking land by joining Indian rivalries, colonists allied with the Narragansetts against the Pequots, who controlled Connecticut territory, and ended the war by burning the main Pequot village, killing hundreds.

column1: Why did Metacom go to war, and why did he lose?
column2: Metacom fought because colonists humiliated the Wampanoags, ruined their fields and split the tribe with praying towns, but he lost when food and ammunition ran short and the Mohegan and Mohawk Indians sided with the English.

column1: How did the English take New Netherland?
column2: The Dutch West India Company had gone bankrupt and virtually abandoned the colony, so the Dutch surrendered on the mere arrival of the Duke of York's invading fleet in 1664.

column1: In what ways were the mid-Atlantic colonies more diverse than other colonies?
column2: The mid-Atlantic mixed Dutch, English, French, Swedes, Finns, Germans, Africans and Jews with Dutch Reformed, Quaker, Lutheran, Catholic and other faiths, lacking New England's common bonds.

column1: How did Penn's Pennsylvania differ from Puritan Massachusetts in religion and Indian relations?
column2: Penn's Frame of Government guaranteed complete freedom of worship, unlike tax-supported, dissenter-expelling Massachusetts, and Penn bought land from the Lenni Lenape (Delaware) Indians before selling it, keeping peace.

column1: How did William and Mary try to increase colonial revenues?
column2: In 1696 they added customs officials in every colony, set up jury-less vice-admiralty courts to try smugglers, and created the Board of Trade, channeling colonial trade through England.

column1: What had the colonies become by 1700, according to the text?
column2: By 1700 the colonies were becoming firmly rooted societies whose laws and traditions rested on both English inheritance and American conditions, which blocked Stuart, proprietor and reformer designs.

column1: Why was royal power in the colonies "more apparent than real" after 1700?
column2: The Glorious Revolution made Parliament supreme in England, and colonial assemblies grew skilled at handling governors and fiercely guarded the lower houses' power to levy taxes.
